info.title: Freestyle
info.description:
# Powerful Virtual Machines

Documentation: [freestyle.sh/docs](https://freestyle.sh/docs)

Freestyle VMs are full Linux virtual machines designed for long running, complex tasks.

## Key Features

- **Instant Startup**: Freestyle VMs provision in milliseconds, with p99s under 400ms.
- **Persistence**: Freestyle VMs can run forever, they can be hibernated with their exact memory in place and come back to life weeks later instantly, in that exact state.
- **Powerful**: Freestyle VMs go up to 64GB of RAM for public tiers and much further for enterprise. Freestyle does high quality hardware virtualization supporting nested virtualization, FUSE, eBPF, full Linux networking and more. If it can run in an EC2, it can run in a Freestyle VM.
- **Cheaply Snapshottable and Branchable**: Freestyle VMs are instantly and cheaply snapshottable (sub 1ms interruption, sub 50ms to snapshot ready). These snapshots can be used to create new VMs in the exact state of the original VM (memory and disk). This enables powerful workflows like branching, cloning, and rapid recovery from failures.

## When to use Freestyle

- **Long Running Agent Tasks**: When you have tasks that take hours, days, weeks or months to run, Freestyle VMs provide a persistent and powerful environment that your agent can work in to completion.
- **Failure Prone/Experimental Exploration**: When your tasks involve branching, cloning or need time travel Freestyle VMs are ideal because of their cheap snapshottability and power that makes them great for experiments.
- **Complex Coding Problems**: When you are tackling advanced coding problems in research or production codebases, poor virtualization and small sandboxes will not cut it. Freestyle VMs provide the necessary resources and environment to handle these challenges effectively.
- **Multi Tenant Usage Patterns**: Freestyle VMs are intentionally built to be used by agent builders with multiple customers. The slug system allows for keying VMs by their user, the identity system allows for granular acccess control and permissioning, and the VPC system allows for multi-tenant network isolation. 

## When not to use it

- **"Run AI Code"**: If your exclusively executing short lived Python scripts or other ephemeral tasks the benefits above aren't relevant. Freestyle VMs should still be benchmarked but there may be alternatives better suited.
- **CPU Intensive CI/CD**: Freestyle VMs run on bare metal on data center CPUs. We also oversubscribe host resources. For workloads that require sustained high CPU usage like building the Linux Kernel or mining crypto prefer cloud providers that offer consumer CPU performance.
- **Short Lived Tasks**: If your tasks are extremely short lived and do not benefit from persistence or powerful hardware. If your average task takes less than 15 minutes to complete then they are likely cheaply retryable and don't require the reliability and persistence that Freestyle VMs provide.
- **Sole Application Hosting**: Freestyle VMs are designed as workbenches for development, experimentation and task execution. Not for hosting production applications. Hosting a minecraft server for some friends will work great on Freestyle, but we do not offer autoscaling, load balancers or CDNs and we don't plan to.

## Emerging Use Cases

- **RL Environments**: Freestyle VMs are well-suited for running reinforcement learning environments that require persistent state and complex setups. The ability to snapshot and branch VMs allows researchers to experiment with different strategies and record environment states efficiently.
- **Auto Research Climbing**: Freestyle VMs are great for auto research as the snapshotting and fan out allows research agents to explore multiple strategies, review past results and iterate efficiently without ever losing progress.
- **Environments for Development, Testing, Security and Pentesting**: Freestyle VMs are the only sandbox provider that offers full private VPC and networking which allows simulating full applications in production like staging environments. This can be used for testing, iteration, security assesments and penetration testing in a controlled and isolated environment.
- **Connecting Agents to Production VPCs**: Freestyle VMs VPC system allows for connections to private production VPCs through secure Wireguard tunnels. If you want sandboxed agents to work on your/your users production infrastructure and they have requirements about not going through the public internet, Freestyle VMs provide a secure and compliant solution.

## Private Offers (Enterprise)

- **GPU Sandboxes**: Freestyle offers private GPU sandboxes for enterprise customers, providing direct access to frontier GPU hardware for high performance computing, machine learning and generally the above **Emerging Use Cases**.
- **Colocated Bare Metal**: For users wanting sandboxes that work with especially weird requirements Freestyle can offer space in our racks for your dedicated bare metal servers. This can be useful for custom GPUs, video processing, or any other specialized hardware needs.
- **Custom Pricing**: Freestyle can offer spot access, CPU Time billing, node based pricing and more. These deals can be tailored to the specific needs and usage patterns of enterprise customers.
- **Custom Sandboxing**: Freestyle builds and maintains its own custom virtualization solutions which allows us to virtualize and sandbox workloads in ways that are not possible with standard options. This enables highly specialized and optimized environments for enterprise customers.
- **Dedicated Support**: Enterprise customers can receive dedicated support from the Freestyle team, ensuring that any issues or custom requirements are addressed promptly and effectively.

For more information on Enterprise offerings contact our [sales team](https://cal.com/freestyle/enterprise-onboarding?overlayCalendar=true)

### Relevant Links

- [Freestyle Documentation](https://freestyle.sh/docs)
- [Freestyle Dashboard](https://dash.freestyle.sh) — manage your account and API keys.

AI agents can create their own API key with `npx -y freestyle@latest tokens create "agent work" --output json` using an existing CLI login. Run `npx -y freestyle@latest login` first if needed, then use the returned `token` as `FREESTYLE_API_KEY`.

get.description:
A request started with the `x-freestyle-background-after-secs` header
answers `202 Accepted` with a `requestId` once that many seconds elapse;
poll this route with it. While the request is still running this answers
`202` again; once it finishes, the request's own response — its status,
headers, and body, success or error — is returned exactly as the original
call would have. Results expire ten minutes after completion; a result
that was delivered inline (the original call returned before the window
elapsed) is not kept here.

post.description:
Switch a physical machine's power.

This is a real power outlet, so it is deliberately narrow. The unit is the whole machine: machines with redundant supplies draw from several cords and all of them are switched together, because cutting one browns the machine out instead of powering it off. `cycle` cuts power, holds a few seconds, and restores it — anything running stops immediately, with no chance to shut down cleanly.

Heavily rate limited: one power-cutting action every few minutes and a small daily budget per machine, both reported by `GET /hardware/{hardwareId}/power`. Turning power back **on** is never rationed, only briefly debounced. Exceeding a limit is a 429 whose message says when to come back.

Send the file as the raw request body (with `?path=`) and it can be as large as 16 GiB — nothing buffers it whole. Send a JSON body instead (up to 32 MiB) when it is easier to type than to upload, as from this page.

This is a single attempt: if the connection drops, the write starts over. To upload something big over a link you do not trust, open an upload session (`POST /fs/uploads`) and send retryable chunks instead.

AccountId.description:
Identifies an account. New accounts are minted by the identity
service's registry as `"acct-<uuid>"`; accounts created before the
prefix era are bare UUID strings, and the built-in `freestyle`
infrastructure account is the literal `"freestyle"`. All three forms
are equally valid ids: the prefix is a minting convention, not a
format requirement.

path.description:
JSON-Pointer value [RFC6901](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6901) that references a location
within the target document where the operation is performed.

value.description: Value to add to the target location.

AttachNetwork.description: Attach a VM to one of your private networks. A VM may be on at most one.

ipv4.description:
The IPv4 address to take inside the network: an explicit address,
`true` to auto-allocate, or `false` to opt out. Omitted = allocate one
(networks are dual-stack), except on a network with no IPv4 CIDR,
where the VM simply joins over IPv6.

ipv6.description:
The IPv6 address to take: an explicit address, `true` to auto-allocate
(the default), or `false` to opt out. Every network has an IPv6 CIDR.

routes.description: Static routes to install in the guest.

vpc.description:
The network to join, by id or by your slug for it. Also accepted as
`vpcId`, the name the rest of the API uses.

exit.description:
Make your client this network's exit — a router members can name as a
next hop. A VM routes through it with an ordinary NIC route via the
attachment's address, and everything it sends the exit — whatever the
destination — is forwarded to your client, which is expected to NAT it
onward. Several attachments per network may be exits: members choose
per route, so two exits and two same-metric routes are a redundant
pair, and a dead exit stops being ARP-answered so the other takes
over by itself.

ipv4.description:
The address you want inside the private network. Omit to be assigned
one. It must be free: a VM already holding it makes this a conflict,
and once yours, no VM can be given it.

ipv6.description:
An explicit IPv6 address, equivalent to passing one in `ipv4`; only one
may be set.

remoteCidrs.description:
Ranges behind your client that this network routes through the tunnel —
a site-to-site setup where your client machine forwards for other hosts
on its side. Hosts inside these ranges keep their real addresses inside
the network. A range carved out of the network's own CIDR just works:
VMs reach it with no configuration, and the range is excluded from VM
address allocation (it must be free when granted). A range outside the
network's CIDRs is reached by giving VMs a route via the attachment's
`address`. A range may not straddle the network's CIDR boundary, nor
overlap a range another tunnel already grants this network.

BackgroundRequestId.description:
Identifies a backgrounded public-API request (the handle a client
polls `/background-requests/{id}` with). Minted as `"bgr-<uuid>"`.

mode.description:
Optional final file mode bits (e.g. 493 for `0o755`). Defaults to the
target's existing mode, or `0o600` for a new file.

path.description: Absolute path inside the guest the finished file is committed to.

sha256.description:
Optional sha256 of the full file as 64 hex characters; the upload is
rejected at commit if the received bytes do not match.

size.description: Total file size in bytes, up to 16 GiB.

exitCode.description:
Exit code if the session had already exited. Absent when it was still
running: it is sent `SIGHUP` and torn down asynchronously.

ContentEncoding.description: How `content` is encoded in the JSON form of a write.

from.description:
JSON-Pointer value [RFC6901](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6901) that references a location
to copy value from.

path.description:
JSON-Pointer value [RFC6901](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6901) that references a location
within the target document where the operation is performed.

action.description: Required, and `allow` is the only accepted value.

description.description: A free-form note, up to 1024 characters.

managed.description:
Create a managed identity. Managed identities cannot be deleted through
the public surface.

autoDeleteSeconds.description:
Delete the snapshot once this many seconds pass without a VM being
created from it. Every create from it resets the clock. -1 (or
omitting this) means never; some plans cap this, and on those omitting
it (or sending -1) gets you the cap.

ttlSeconds.description:
Delete the snapshot this many seconds after it is taken, whatever has
booted it since. -1 (or omitting this) means no deadline.

CreateTlsForwardAuthRequest.description: Create or replace a reusable HTTP authorization pre-check.

authResponseHeaders.description: Headers copied from a successful check onto the VM request.

headers.description: Static headers added to the check. Values are write-only.

protectedCookies.description: Cookie names visible to the check but withheld from the VM.

timeoutMs.description: Per-check deadline in milliseconds. Defaults to 1500; range 100-5000.

url.description: Absolute HTTPS endpoint receiving a bodyless GET before the VM request.

action.description: Required, and `allow` is the only accepted value.

description.description: A free-form note, up to 1024 characters.

domain.description: The name the session is addressed to: exact, `*.suffix`, or `*`.

oneOf.description: Run this reusable authorization check before forwarding to the VM.

Vercel-style method/exact-path selector for HTTP egress transforms.
Non-matching requests pass through without any transform.

How the edge treats the bytes. Optional: inferred from `transform` when
one is present, and `tcp` (opaque) otherwise.

transform.description: Rewrites applied in flight, in order. Secrets here are write-only.

clientPublicKey.description:
The public key of a keypair you already hold. Omit to have one minted
for you; supply it and the platform never sees a private key at all.

displayName.description: A free-form label, for telling several tunnels apart.

routes.description:
The ranges your client will route through the tunnel — its
`AllowedIPs`, fixed for the tunnel's life so attaching and detaching
networks never changes your config. Omit for the default
(`10.0.0.0/8` and `fd00::/8`), which covers every network with
default addressing. Only networks whose CIDRs fall inside the routes
can be attached.

slug.description:
A URL-safe handle, unique within your account: 1–63 chars of
`[a-z0-9-]`, no leading, trailing, or repeated hyphens. Address the
tunnel by it instead of by id.

vpcs.description:
Networks to attach in the same call, so one request yields a tunnel
that already routes somewhere. All-or-nothing: if any attachment is
refused, nothing is created.

CreateTunnelVpc.description: One network named at create, with the same address choices as an attach.

ipv4.description: The address you want inside it; omit to be assigned one.

ipv6.description: An explicit IPv6 address instead; only one may be set.

remoteCidrs.description:
Ranges behind your client this network may route to; see the attach
request's `remoteCidrs`.

vpc.description:
The network to attach: a VPC id, or your slug for it. Also accepted as
`vpcId`.

autoDeleteSeconds.description:
Delete the VM once it has gone this many seconds without running.
Every start resets the clock; a running VM is never deleted for this.
-1 (or omitting this) means never; 0 makes the VM ephemeral — deleted
the moment it stops.

Some plans cap how long an unused VM is kept. On those, omitting this
(or sending -1) gets you the cap rather than "keep forever", and asking
for longer than the cap is a 400.

automaticRestart.description:
Boot the VM again if it stops without you asking it to — the VMM
crashes, the guest kernel panics, the machine it runs on loses power.
Defaults to `true`.

It never fights you: shutting the VM down, pausing it, running
`poweroff` inside it, or hitting an idle timeout all leave it off. This
only decides who gets the last word when a *failure* stops it.

firewall.description:
Firewall rules to create with the VM, and delete with it. An endpoint
with no identity means the VM being created, so `{ "source": { "public":
true }, "destination": { "port": 443, "protocol": "tcp" } }` opens
inbound HTTPS to it.

**Required.** A VM gets nothing implicitly — no outbound Internet, no
inbound — so a caller that wants either says so here. `{"rules": []}` is
a legitimate answer: a VM reachable only through a mapped domain or SSH.

idleTimeoutSeconds.description:
Pause the VM after this many seconds without network activity.
-1 (or omitting this) means never pause for idleness.

maxRunSeconds.description:
Pause the VM once a single run has lasted this many seconds, however
busy it is. Starting it again gives it a fresh budget — unlike
`maxRunTotalSeconds`, which never resets. -1 (or omitting this) means
no cap.

maxRunTotalSeconds.description:
How many seconds this VM may run in total, ever. Spending the budget
pauses the VM, and every later start is a 409 until you raise this.
-1 (or omitting this) means no budget.

metadata.description: Up to 64 metadata entries; keys and values are limited to 63 characters.

networks.description:
Put the VM on your private networks. Omit to leave it off them. At most
one network is accepted today. Also accepted as `vpcs`, the name the
rest of the API uses.

reassignSlug.description:
Take `slug` even if another VM in this account already holds it. The
slug moves atomically: the current holder keeps running, stays
addressable by id, and just loses its slug. Without this flag a taken
slug is a 409 CONFLICT. Requires `slug`.

slug.description:
URL-safe identifier, unique within your account: 1–63 chars of
`[a-z0-9-]`, no leading, trailing, or repeated hyphens.

snapshotId.description:
Boot from this snapshot: its id, your slug for it, or a public
`{owner}/{slug}`. Omit for the platform default.

oneOf.description:
TLS rules to create with the VM, and delete with it — named sessions the
VM may serve or open. An endpoint with no identity means the VM being
created, so `{ "action": "allow", "domain": "app.acme.com", "source":
{ "public": true }, "destination": { "port": 8000 } }` publishes that
domain to it.

Optional, unlike `firewall`: a TLS rule is a grant layered on top of the
firewall's packet decision, never a baseline a VM must state. The created
rules come back on the response as `tlsRules`, with the ids a later
delete needs.

ttlSeconds.description:
Delete the VM this many seconds after it is created, whatever it is
doing at the time. A deadline, not an idle window: nothing resets it.
-1 (or omitting this) means no deadline.

cidr.description:
The network's IPv4 CIDR. Networks are dual-stack; a `/24` out of
`10.0.0.0/8` is derived for you when omitted. Name one to choose the
range yourself — worth doing when the network has to reach an existing
estate over a tunnel and must not overlap it, or when it needs more
than 254 IPv4 members.

cidrV6.description:
The network's IPv6 CIDR; a unique-local /64 is derived for you when
omitted.

oneOf.description:
Firewall rules created with the network and deleted with it. A bare
endpoint means the network being created, so
`{"source":{},"destination":{}}` is "members reach each other".

CreatedTunnel.description:
A tunnel plus a client private key. Returned by the two calls that mint a
keypair — create and rotate-key — and nowhere else: the key is never stored
and cannot be read back. Empty when you supplied your own public key.

recordName.description: Place `verificationCode` in a TXT record at this name, then verify.

verifiedAt.description: When this challenge proved control; null while pending.

DomainVerificationId.description: Identifies a domain-verification challenge. Minted as `"dv-<uuid>"`.

DomainVerified.description:
A successful verification: ownership, plus which challenge proved it.
Several users may hold challenges for one domain, so `verifiedBy` names the
one whose code was published.

command.description: The command line, run through the guest's shell.

env.description: Extra environment variables. Keys must be valid POSIX names.

oneOf.description:
Existing in-guest Linux user to run the command as. Omit for the guest's default user:
whoever holds uid 1000, or root in an image that has no such account.

stdin.description: Base64-encoded stdin, up to 1 MiB decoded.

timeoutMs.description:
Wall-clock limit, milliseconds. 1–300000; defaults to 30000 (30 s).
The guest kills the command at the deadline.

statusCode.description: The command's exit status; absent if it was killed by the timeout.

FirewallAction.description:
What a rule does with the traffic it matches.

Only `allow` exists today, and it is required on every rule rather than
defaulted: a default would mean that the day `deny` arrives, every rule
written before it silently acquires an action it never stated.

FirewallDecision.description:
Why a connection would be allowed, or that it would not.

`outcome` is `allowedByPlatform` (Freestyle's own ingress, e.g. a mapped
domain — no rule involved), `allowedByRule` (with the `ruleId` that
matched), `deniedByPlatform` (with the `reason`, e.g. `outboundMail`, that
no rule can override), or `denied`.

reason.description: Which platform policy closed it, on `deniedByPlatform`.

side.description: Which end was Freestyle's ingress, on `allowedByPlatform`.

FirewallDependency.description: A resource a rule cannot outlive: deleting it deletes the rule.

displayName.description: Your label for the named resource, under the same rules as `slug`.

kind.description: `vm`, `vpc`, or `tunnel` today. New selectors add new kinds.

slug.description:
Your handle for the named resource, when it has one — so a rule says
what it points at without a lookup per id.

FirewallEndpoint.description:
One end of a rule: which traffic this side matches.

Fields intersect — `{ vpcId, port, protocol }` is "traffic in that network,
on that port, over that protocol". `vmId`/`vpcId`/`tunnelId` select by
identity (the VM however it is addressed); `cidr`/`public` select by
address. Unknown fields
are rejected rather than ignored: a matcher is a security statement, and a
typo'd `porrt: 22` that quietly became "every port" is the wrong failure.

cidr.description: An address range, IPv4 or IPv6, in canonical `network/prefix` form.

tunnelId.description:
Whatever is on the far side of one tunnel — the client that dials it,
and any remote range routed over it. Tunnels have no slug, so this is a
tunnel id: `tun-…`, or `wg-…` for one carried over from the per-VPC VPN
records tunnels replaced.

vmId.description: A single VM, by id or by your slug for it. Answers hold its id.

vpcId.description:
Everything on one private network, by id or by your slug for it.
Answers hold its id.

FirewallProtocol.description: The transport a matcher is restricted to.

FirewallRule.description:
An allowed path through the network, as intent: traffic matching `source`
may reach `destination`.

dependencies.description:
What this rule depends on. Deleting any of them deletes this rule, so
no rule is ever left pointing at something that no longer exists.

FirewallSpec.description:
The `firewall` block of a create: rules created with the resource and
deleted with it. Inside it, an endpoint with no identity means the resource
being created — which is how a rule names something whose id does not exist
yet.

allowedLinuxUsers.description:
Restrict the grant to these Linux users; omit (or null) for
unrestricted access.

HardwarePowerAction.description:
What to do to a machine's power.

The unit is always the whole machine. A machine with redundant supplies
draws from several cords, and Freestyle switches all of them together —
there is no way to ask for one, because cutting one cord browns a machine
out rather than powering it off.

HardwarePowerState.description: A machine's power, and what is left of its rate limit.

cords.description: How many power cords feed it — why control is all-or-nothing.

message.description: Why the power state is unknown, when it is.

nextAllowedAt.description: When the next power-cutting action will be accepted. Absent means now.

on.description:
Every cord is live. Absent when the power state could not be read —
which is not the same as the machine being off.

remainingToday.description:
Power-cutting actions left in the rolling 24-hour budget. Turning power
**on** does not spend it.

supported.description:
False when power control is not enabled for this machine; every other
field is then absent and every action is refused.

watts.description: Present draw across the machine's cords, in watts.

HardwareServer.description:
A physical machine attached to one of your private networks.

Freestyle racks and cables these, so there is no create or delete here —
what the API offers is seeing them and, where it is enabled, controlling
their power.

attached.description: The network attachment is converged and the machine is being served.

dhcpBound.description:
The machine has taken a DHCP lease — the closest thing to "it is on"
that the network can see by itself.

ipv4.description: Its address on the private network, when that network carries IPv4.

ipv6.description: Its address on the private network. Every network has IPv6.

lastSeen.description: When the network last saw traffic from it.

mac.description: The machine's MAC, once it is known.

powerControl.description:
Whether this machine's power can be switched through the API. Off
unless Freestyle has enabled it for the machine.

publicIpv6.description: Its stable public address, when it was given one.

vpcId.description: The private network the machine is attached to.

HttpPathMatch.description: Exact request path. Prefix and regex matching are not supported yet.

HttpRequestMatch.description:
Select which HTTP egress requests receive a rule's transforms.
Included dimensions are ANDed; methods are ORed. An empty object matches all.
A non-match skips every transform, without denying access to the origin.
See <https://vercel.com/docs/sandbox/concepts/firewall#matchers>.

method.description: Case-sensitive HTTP method tokens. Omitted matches any; an empty list matches none.

oneOf.description: Case-sensitive path comparison, excluding the query string.

IdentityId.description:
Identifies an identity (the auth principal under an account). Minted
as `"idn-<uuid>"`.

IdentityTokenId.description: Identifies an identity access token row. Minted as `"tok-<uuid>"`.

JsonPatch.description:
Ordered RFC 6902 operations. Values are write-only and read back as `"***"`.
A rule accepts one patch, with at most 128 operations and 64 KiB of configuration.

LinuxUserId.description:
Branded POSIX-style Linux username carried as `linuxUser` in JSON bodies
and query strings. Constructed only via
`try_from`/`from_str`, which enforces the same rule as
`freestyle-firecracker/models/src/users.rs::is_valid_posix_name`:
`[a-z_][a-z0-9_-]*` up to `MAX_LEN` chars.

Validating at the type boundary keeps shell metacharacters and oversized
values out of the host node and prevents them from reaching the guest.

tunnels.description:
Newest first. Listings never carry a private key; the config returned
here has `PrivateKey` blanked.

MakeDirRequest.description:
The public mkdir body. The internal API takes a bare `{path}` here while its
sibling `remove` takes a query parameter; the public surface keeps the same

NetworkRoute.description:
An in-guest static route: reach `cidr` via the gateway `via`, which must be
an address inside the network's CIDR.

metric.description:
Route priority, as `ip route`'s `metric`. Omit for the platform
default. Several routes to the same `cidr` at the same metric are one
multipath route — the guest spreads flows across their gateways —
while different metrics make a primary and a backup.

'remove' operation
'replace' operation

'test' operation

PlaceholderBranding.description:
What your placeholder pages wear: the edge's 404 for a hostname under one of
your verified domains that none of your TLS rules serve.

logoUrl.description: An https URL of the logo. The visitor's browser loads it directly.

productName.description: Named on the page in place of Freestyle. Null = logo only.

PostgresTransform.description:
Credentials injected into a Postgres startup handshake. The guest connects
with no password; the edge completes the real handshake upstream.

database.description: The database to select. Optional: omitted leaves the guest's choice.

password.description: The upstream password. Write-only: sealed at rest, read back as `"***"`.

username.description: The upstream role to authenticate as.

PtySession.description:
One interactive terminal session. Sessions are owned by the guest agent and
outlive the connection that opened them: dropping the WebSocket only
detaches, so the shell keeps running and a later client can reattach. An
exited session stays listable and attachable briefly, so a client can still
read the final output and exit code.

createdUnix.description: Unix timestamp, in seconds, when the session was opened.

exitCode.description: Exit code, present only once the session has exited.

linuxUser.description: Linux user the session runs as. Absent means the guest default, root.

sessionId.description: Per-VM session id, for attaching or closing this session.

slug.description:
The name this session was opened with, while it still answers to it.
Released as soon as the shell exits, so an exited session reports none
and is addressable only by `sessionId`.

state.description: `running` while the shell is alive, `exited` once it has terminated.

PublicErrorBody.description:
The shape of every error response: a stable machine-readable `code` and a
human-readable `message`. The HTTP status carries the class of failure.

Some errors add fields alongside these two; `code` and `message` are always
present.

code.description:
A stable identifier for the failure, in `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE`. Branch
on this; `message` is prose and may be reworded at any time.

message.description:
A human-readable explanation of what went wrong. A fault inside the
platform is always reported as `INTERNAL_ERROR` with no further detail.

path.description:
JSON-Pointer value [RFC6901](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6901) that references a location
within the target document where the operation is performed.

storage.description: Disk, MiB. Disks can only grow.

clientPublicKey.description:
The public key of a keypair you already hold. Omit to have a fresh one
minted for you.

prefix.description: Literal UTF-8 key prefix, including a trailing slash for a directory boundary.

logoUrl.description: An https URL of the logo, at most 2048 characters.

productName.description:
Named on the page in place of Freestyle, at most 64 characters. Omit
for logo only.

Snapshot.description:
A snapshot as its owner sees it. The disk/memory layer tree, replication
targets, and originating manager are storage internals and are not exposed.

autoDeleteFromPlan.description:
Whether `autoDeleteSeconds` above is your plan's doing rather than
yours, under the same rule as on a VM.

autoDeleteSeconds.description:
Delete the snapshot once this long has passed without a VM being
created from it. Absent means never. Some plans cap this and the cap
shows up here.

lastUsedAt.description:
When a VM was last created from this snapshot. Absent if none ever has
been — which is not the same as never having been touched, since
renaming a snapshot is not using it.

public.description: Public snapshots are bootable by any account.

sourceVmDisplayName.description: The source VM's display name now, under the same rules.

sourceVmSlug.description:
What the source VM is called *now*; absent when it has no slug and
when it is gone.

ttlSeconds.description:
Delete the snapshot this long after it was taken, however recently
anything booted it.

Socks5Transform.description:
Credentials presented to an upstream SOCKS5 proxy. Your VM connects to the
platform's SOCKS5 front with no authentication at all; the edge authenticates
to your provider on its behalf, so the subscription is never inside the VM.

password.description:
The password to present to the upstream proxy. Write-only: sealed at
rest, read back as `"***"`.

username.description: The username to present to the upstream proxy.

path.description:
JSON-Pointer value [RFC6901](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6901) that references a location
within the target document where the operation is performed.

TlsAction.description:
What a rule does with the named session it matches.

Only `allow` exists today, and it is required on every rule rather than
defaulted: a default would mean that the day `deny` arrives, every rule
written before it silently acquires an action it never stated.

TlsDependency.description: A resource a rule cannot outlive: deleting it deletes the rule.

displayName.description: Your label for the named resource, under the same rules as `slug`.

kind.description: `vm` or `vpc` today. New selectors add new kinds.

slug.description:
Your handle for the named resource, when it has one — so a rule says
what it points at without a lookup per id.

TlsEndpoint.description:
One end of a rule: which session this side matches.

A `source` says *who* may open the session (`vmId`/`vpcId`/`public: true`); a
`destination` says *where it lands* (`vmId`+`port`, `host`+`port`, or
`public: true` for the domain's own origin). Unknown fields are rejected
rather than ignored: a rule is a security statement, and a typo that quietly
widened it is the wrong failure.

host.description:
**Destination only.** Pin the session to this host instead of resolving
the domain, while still presenting `domain` as the SNI.

port.description:
**Destination only.** The port the session lands on. Required with a
`vmId` or `host` destination; defaults to 443 for a `public` origin.

public.description:
On a source, every publicly routable client — the open Internet dials the
name. On a destination, the domain's own public origin. Only `true` is
meaningful; omit the field otherwise.

vmId.description:
A single VM, by id or by your slug for it. On a source, the VM that may
open the session; on a destination, the VM it lands on. Answers hold its id.

vpcId.description:
Everything on one private network, by id or by your slug for it. **Source
only** — a landing is one place, so a network cannot be a destination.
Answers hold its id.

TlsForwardAuth.description: A stored forward-auth configuration. Static header values are redacted.

TlsForwardAuthReference.description: A reusable authorization check attached to public HTTP ingress.

TlsProtocolDocumented.description:
How the edge treats the session's bytes, and therefore which of its front
doors serves the rule.

`http` (443) and `postgres` (5432) terminate the session, so each pairs with
the transform kind that speaks it and each needs a certificate for the name.
`minecraft` (25565) routes on the server address in the client's handshake
and then splices — no TLS, so no certificate and no transform.

The other two doors carry a terminating protocol and a splicing one at once,
and a rule picks which it is. `tcp` shares 443 with `http`: match on SNI,
splice the bytes, terminate nothing, so your VM's own certificate answers the
handshake. `imap` and `imaps` share 993 for mail clients — `imap` terminates
on a certificate issued for the name and forwards plain IMAP to the port your
server listens on (143 by default), `imaps` splices to a server holding its
own certificate on 993. All three splicing shapes are public ingress only.

`socks5` (1080) goes the other way and is the only egress-only protocol. Your
VM opens SOCKS5 to the platform edge with no authentication, names its own
destination inside the request, and the edge opens the session onward through
your proxy provider using the credentials a `socks5` transform carries — so
the workload can use the subscription without ever holding it. Nothing is
terminated: your TLS runs end to end to the real origin. The rule's `domain`
is an allow-list of destinations rather than a name anything resolves, which
is why `*` is allowed here and refused everywhere else.

TlsRule.description:
An allowed named session over a domain, as intent: a session addressed to
`domain`, from `source`, to `destination`, with any in-flight `transform`.

dependencies.description:
What this rule depends on. Deleting any of them deletes this rule, so no
rule is ever left pointing at something that no longer exists.

domain.description: The name the session is addressed to: exact, `*.suffix`, or `*`.

oneOf.description: Optional reusable authorization check for public HTTP ingress.

Vercel-style method/exact-path selector for HTTP egress transforms.
Non-matching requests pass through without any transform.

redacted.description:
Whether any transform secret was redacted out of `transform`, so you know
the shape you see is not the whole story.

transform.description: The rewrites this rule applies, with every secret replaced by `"***"`.

TlsSpec.description:
The `tls` block of a VM create: rules created with the VM and deleted with
it. Inside it, an endpoint with no identity means the VM being created —
which is how a rule names a VM whose id does not exist yet.

oneOf.description:
Set request headers on an `http` session. Header names are preserved
(they are not secret); values are write-only.

headers.description:
Set request headers on an `http` session. Header names are preserved
(they are not secret); values are write-only.

oneOf.description:
Apply RFC 6902 operations to JSON HTTP egress request bodies.
Values are write-only; operation names and JSON Pointer paths remain visible.

jsonPatch.description:
Apply RFC 6902 operations to JSON HTTP egress request bodies.
Values are write-only; operation names and JSON Pointer paths remain visible.

oneOf.description: Inject credentials into a `postgres` handshake.
Authenticate a `socks5` session to your upstream proxy provider.

socks5.description: Authenticate a `socks5` session to your upstream proxy provider.

oneOf.description: Authorize and sign scoped S3 HTTP requests at the edge.

s3.description: Authorize and sign scoped S3 HTTP requests at the edge.

TlsTransformDocumented.description: The rewrites a rule applies, in order.

TrafficParty.description:
One end of a connection to ask about: everything true about the party, not
a pattern.

address.description: The address in use, when there is one — what `cidr` rules are tested against.

platform.description:
Freestyle's own ingress — the web proxy serving a mapped domain, or the
SSH proxy. Always allowed, whatever the rules say.

public.description: Whether that address is publicly routable — what `public: true` matches.

vpcIds.description: Every private network this party is on; a rule naming one of them matches.

Tunnel.description:
A tunnel: your WireGuard identity on the platform. It exists until you
delete it: connect, disconnect and reconnect as often as you like — a
session is set up on the handshake that needs it, so an idle tunnel costs
nothing and never expires. A tunnel routes nowhere until you attach a
private network to it; attach several and one WireGuard interface reaches
them all.

attachments.description: The private networks on the far side, oldest attachment first.

clientAddressV4.description:
Your fixed addresses inside the tunnel. Only the gateway ever sees
them: each attached network sees an address inside its own subnet
instead (`attachments[].address`).

clientConfig.description:
A complete WireGuard config file, fixed for the life of the tunnel:
attaching and detaching networks never changes it, so bring it up once
and manage what it reaches through the API. `PrivateKey` is blank
except on create and rotate-key, the only two responses that mint a
keypair.

displayName.description: Your label for this tunnel, if you gave it one.

id.description: Deprecated: the tunnel's id under its old name. Read `tunnelId`.

routes.description:
The ranges your client routes through the tunnel — its `AllowedIPs`,
fixed at create. A network can only be attached if its CIDRs fall
inside these.

serverPublicKey.description: The one `[Peer]` public key in your config.

slug.description:
Your handle for this tunnel, if you gave it one. Usable anywhere the id
is, in place of it.

tunnelId.description:
The tunnel's id, under the name the rest of the API uses for it — a
firewall rule says `tunnelId`, so the tunnel does too.

TunnelAttachment.description:
One private network on the far side of a tunnel: the network, your address
inside it, and the `[Peer]` key that carries it.

address.description: Deprecated: the primary address, whichever family. Read `ipv4`/`ipv6`.

allowedIps.description: The CIDRs the gateway routes to this network.

exit.description:
Whether this attachment is a network exit: your client forwards for
destinations that are not its own address, and members route through
it with an ordinary route via the attachment's address. Omitted when
false.

ipv4.description:
Your IPv4 address inside the private network, absent on a v6-only
attachment. It belongs to this tunnel for as long as the network stays
attached, so you can write it into configs and rules.

ipv6.description: Your IPv6 address inside the private network, under the same rules.

remoteCidrs.description:
Ranges behind your client that this network routes through the tunnel
(a site-to-site grant). VMs reach them with an ordinary route via
`address`. Omitted when the attachment has none.

allowedLinuxUsers.description: The new allowed-Linux-users list; null grants unrestricted access.

autoDeleteSeconds.description:
Seconds of nothing being created from it before the snapshot is
deleted; -1 removes the window. On a plan that caps it, -1 puts you
back on the cap rather than off it.

ttlSeconds.description:
Seconds from when the snapshot was taken — not from now — before it is
deleted; -1 removes the deadline.

UpdateVmNetworksRequest.description:
The desired network set for `PUT /vms/{vmIdOrSlug}/networks`. Declarative:
what is listed is attached, what is absent is detached.

networks.description:
At most one network is accepted today. An empty list detaches the VM.
Also accepted as `vpcs`, the name the rest of the API uses.

autoDeleteSeconds.description:
Seconds of not running before the VM is deleted; -1 removes the window
(on a plan that caps it, -1 puts you back on the cap rather than off
it), and 0 makes the VM ephemeral — deleted the moment it stops, or
right away if it is already stopped.

automaticRestart.description:
Turn automatic restart on or off. Applies to the next failure: this
neither boots a stopped VM nor stops a running one.

displayName.description: Change the display label; an empty string clears it.

idleTimeoutSeconds.description: Seconds of network idleness before pause; -1 removes the timeout.

maxRunSeconds.description: Seconds one run may last before the VM is paused; -1 removes the cap.

maxRunTotalSeconds.description:
The lifetime runtime budget in seconds; -1 removes it. Raising this
past `totalRunSeconds` is how you start a VM that spent its budget.

metadata.description:
Metadata merged into the VM. Only the keys you send are touched; send an
empty value to remove one.

reassignSlug.description:
Take `slug` even if another VM in this account already holds it. The
slug moves atomically: the current holder keeps running, stays
addressable by id, and just loses its slug. Without this flag a taken
slug is a 409 CONFLICT. Requires a non-empty `slug`.

slug.description: Change the slug; an empty string clears it.

ttlSeconds.description:
Seconds from creation — not from now — before the VM is deleted; -1
removes the deadline. A value already in the past deletes it shortly.

path.description: Absolute guest path the file will be committed to.

receivedBytes.description: Bytes stored so far — the offset the next chunk must start at.

size.description: Total declared file size in bytes.

VerificationState.description:
Where a challenge stands. A challenge is not consumed by success: it
becomes the durable record of which user proved control.

Vm.description:
A VM as the owning account sees it. Placement and topology internals
(hosting manager, VXLAN ids, node-local network allocation) are not part of
this contract.

autoDeleteFromPlan.description:
Whether `autoDeleteSeconds` above is your plan's doing rather than
yours. A window your plan set goes away by itself if you move to a plan
that does not reclaim unused VMs; one you set is yours and stays.

autoDeleteSeconds.description:
Delete the VM once it has gone this long without running. Absent means
never; 0 means the VM is ephemeral — deleted the moment it stops. Note
that this may be set for you: some plans cap how long an unused VM is
kept, and the cap shows up here.

automaticRestart.description: Whether the VM is booted again when it stops without being asked to.

egressIpv4.description:
The public IPv4 address the VM's outbound traffic is seen as coming
from. It belongs to your account rather than to this VM: every VM you
own shares it, and it survives restarts and moves between machines.

Optional, and worth reading as optional even though a VM in service
has one: nothing promises an account keeps a single outbound address,
so allow for it being absent rather than depending on it being there.

egressIpv6.description:
The public IPv6 address the VM's outbound traffic is seen as coming
from. Today it is the VM's own `publicIpv6` — it appears from the
address it answers on — but read it as its own field: where a VM
answers and where it appears from are two questions, and `egressIpv4`
above already answers them differently.

image.description: The image the VM booted from, when it booted from one.

maxRunSeconds.description: Pause the VM once one run has lasted this long, however busy it is.

maxRunTotalSeconds.description:
The VM's lifetime runtime budget in seconds. Spending it pauses the VM
and makes every later start a 409 until you raise this.

networks.description: Deprecated: the same list as `vpcs`, kept for old readers.

oneOf.description: The placement constraints the VM was created with, when any.

publicIpv6.description:
The VM's stable public IPv6 address — assigned at create and kept for
the VM's life, across restarts and moves between machines.

slug.description: URL-safe identifier, unique within the account; usable anywhere an id is.

oneOf.description: The snapshot the VM booted from, when it booted from one.

sourceSnapshotDisplayName.description: The snapshot's display name now, under the same rules.

sourceSnapshotSlug.description:
What that snapshot is called *now* — its own slug, unqualified. Absent
when it has no slug and when it is gone, so read against
`sourceSnapshotSlugAtCreate` a renamed origin tells apart from a
deleted one.

sourceSnapshotSlugAtCreate.description:
What that snapshot was called when the VM was created, qualified
`{owner}/{slug}` when it belongs to another account. A name, not a
pointer: slugs move, so boot from `snapshotId`, not from this.

totalRunSeconds.description:
Seconds this VM has spent running, across every run it has ever had.
What `maxRunTotalSeconds` is measured against.

ttlSeconds.description: Delete the VM this long after it was created, whatever it is doing.

VmAntiAffinityRule.description:
One anti-affinity rule: "not on the same `topology` domain as any VM
matching `selector`". At most 8 rules per VM.

VmLabelSelector.description:
Selects VMs by their metadata: a VM matches when its metadata contains
every `matchLabels` entry. At least 1 and at most 8 entries; keys and
values are limited to 63 characters, like the metadata they match.

VmNetwork.description: A VM's place on a private network.

ipv4.description:
The VM's IPv4 address inside the network; absent when the member opted
out of IPv4, or the network has no IPv4 CIDR.

ipv6.description: The VM's IPv6 address, when the network has an IPv6 CIDR.

vpc.description: Deprecated: the network's id under its old name. Read `vpcId`.

vpcDisplayName.description: The network's display name now, under the same rules.

oneOf.description:
The network's id, under the name the rest of the API uses. Filled on
the way out.

vpcSlug.description:
What the network is called *now*. Absent when it has no slug and when
it is gone, so read against `vpcSlugAtAttach` a renamed network tells
apart from a deleted one.

vpcSlugAtAttach.description:
Your slug for the network when the VM was attached to it, if it had one.

A convenience for reading an answer back — `vpc` is the id, and the id is
what to store or compare. It keeps naming what the VM was attached by
after a rename, so this is not a way to find the network again.

VmPermissionId.description: Identifies a VM-permission grant row. Minted as `"vmp-<uuid>"`.

VmPlacement.description:
Placement constraints for a VM, fixed at create time and honored again
whenever the platform relocates the VM.

antiAffinity.description:
Hard rules: the VM will not land on a topology domain already hosting
a VM matched by any rule's selector.

VmPlacementTopology.description:
The topology domain an anti-affinity rule spreads across. `node` — the
only domain today — means "not on the same host machine".

Vpc.description: A private network. Its VXLAN id is a cluster internal and is not published.

cidr.description:
The network's IPv4 CIDR block, when it has one. Networks are
IPv6-first; IPv4 is opt-in at create.

cidrV6.description: The network's IPv6 CIDR block — always present.

VpcIpReservation.description: One reserved address inside a private network.

owner.description:
Who holds the address: a VM id, or `wireguard:{attachmentId}` for a
tunnel attachment's address.

WriteFileRequest.description:
The JSON form of a write: convenient from a docs page or a shell, capped at
32 MiB. Larger files go as raw bytes on the same endpoint.

oneOf.description: Defaults to `utf8`.

sha256.description: Optional sha256 of the file as 64 hex characters.

apiKey.description: Your Freestyle API key, sent as `Authorization: Bearer <api key>`. Every request needs one unless it is authenticated with an identity access token instead.

identityAccessToken.name: x-freestyle-identity-access-token
identityAccessToken.description: An access token belonging to an identity you created. It reaches only the VMs that identity has been granted, and only their exec and terminal routes. Hand one to an end user instead of your API key.
